title: The X3DH Key Agreement Protocol
note: Asynchronous authenticated key agreement using signed and one-time prekeys held by a server; claims mutual authentication, forward secrecy and cryptographic deniability; the spec itself notes that without a one-time prekey the initial key SK is exposed by later compromise of the identity and signed prekey (mitigated by frequent signed-prekey replacement and a following ratchet), that prekey compromise enables key-compromise impersonation, replay of the initial message, and a malicious server or party draining one-time prekeys; no post-compromise security (that comes from the Double Ratchet).
bitmessage_link: Replaces Bitmessage's static-key encryption (one long-lived recipient key, no forward secrecy) with ephemeral and prekey DH; but needs a prekey server, which Bitmessage's flooding design lacks.

title: The Double Ratchet Algorithm
venue: Signal specification, revision 1 2016-11-20; saved copy is revision 4 (2025-11-04)
note: Symmetric-key ratchet (per-message keys, forward secrecy) plus DH ratchet (fresh DH on each reply, post-compromise security / self-healing); handles skipped and out-of-order messages with a bounded skipped-key store; no deniability or metadata protection of its own.
bitmessage_link: The missing piece in Bitmessage: per-message keys and self-healing after key compromise, which a static recipient key cannot give. Needs an ordered pairwise session, which broadcast flooding does not provide.

title: The PQXDH Key Agreement Protocol
note: X3DH plus a signed (last-resort and one-time) KEM prekey, so session keys stay secret against a later quantum adversary (post-quantum forward secrecy against harvest-now-decrypt-later); authentication still rests on discrete log (not post-quantum); keeps a form of cryptographic deniability.
bitmessage_link: Shows what a post-quantum upgrade of static-key messaging looks like: encapsulate to the recipient's KEM prekey, mix with classical DH. Bitmessage's recipient addresses embed a single classical key and have no upgrade path.

title: The Sesame Algorithm: Session Management for Asynchronous Message Encryption
note: Manages many pairwise ratchet sessions per user across multiple devices (user records, device records, session records, expiry of stale sessions); handles session-state divergence and device add/remove; inherits forward secrecy and post-compromise properties from the sessions it manages (X3DH and Double Ratchet) and relies on users to authenticate identity keys out of band (no cryptographic guarantee about who is on the other end without that); the spec discusses device compromise, key-compromise impersonation via compromised signed prekeys, and a server that forces X3DH without one-time prekeys.
bitmessage_link: Bitmessage has one address key per identity and no device concept; multi-device messaging with per-session keys needs this kind of session bookkeeping on top of the ratchet.

title: The XEdDSA and VXEdDSA Signature Schemes
note: EdDSA-compatible signatures made with X25519/X448 identity keys, so one key serves both DH and signing (used to sign prekeys in X3DH); VXEdDSA adds a verifiable random function; no post-quantum security.
bitmessage_link: Bitmessage keeps separate signing and encryption keys per address; XEdDSA shows the single-key alternative Signal uses for prekey signatures.

title: The ML-KEM Braid Protocol (Sparse Post-Quantum Ratchet specification)
note: Sparse continuous key agreement (SCKA) built on ML-KEM that spreads encapsulation keys and ciphertexts over many messages (erasure coding); claims post-quantum forward secrecy and post-compromise security that carry into the Double Ratchet when mixed in (the 'triple ratchet'); symmetric performance trade-off is bandwidth, not extra round trips.
bitmessage_link: Post-quantum healing for an ongoing pairwise session; irrelevant to Bitmessage's one-shot encryption but shows the bandwidth cost of keeping PCS post-quantum, which matters for flooded networks that pay per byte.

title: Signal Protocol and Post-Quantum Ratchets
note: Announces the Sparse Post-Quantum Ratchet and explains the design: ML-KEM ratchet state machine, key/ciphertext chunking, mixed into the classical ratchet; goals are forward secrecy and post-compromise security against quantum adversaries, with hybrid security (secure if either ratchet holds).
bitmessage_link: Deployment account of post-quantum session security at scale; contrast with Bitmessage's single static key per address.

title: Quantum Resistance and the Signal Protocol
note: Announces PQXDH: hybrid X25519 plus CRYSTALS-Kyber (later ML-KEM) key agreement at session start to resist harvest-now-decrypt-later; explains that authentication remains classical.
bitmessage_link: Context for the threat that recorded Bitmessage ciphertexts (every node stores them for days) face from harvest-now-decrypt-later.

title: Advanced cryptographic ratcheting
venue: Open Whisper Systems blog, 2013-11-26 (the Axolotl ratchet announcement)
note: First public description of the Axolotl ratchet (later Double Ratchet): OTR-style DH ratchet combined with hash ratchet so that asynchronous transports get forward secrecy and recovery from key compromise ('self-healing') without waiting for a reply round trip.
bitmessage_link: Published one year after Bitmessage; the design answer to Bitmessage's lack of forward secrecy and compromise recovery on an asynchronous, store-and-forward transport.

title: Technology preview: Sealed sender for Signal
note: Hides the sender identity from the Signal server by putting it inside the end-to-end encrypted envelope; the server still sees the recipient and IP address, and abuse is limited by an unidentified-access delivery token derived from the recipient's profile key; claims sender-identity metadata protection only, not recipient or network-level anonymity.
bitmessage_link: Bitmessage hides the recipient by flooding; sealed sender hides the sender but exposes the recipient to the server, the opposite split. Delivery tokens are the analogue of Bitmessage's proof-of-work admission.

title: iMessage with PQ3: The new state of the art in quantum-secure messaging at scale
note: Hybrid post-quantum (Kyber-1024/ML-KEM plus P-256) initial key establishment and a periodic post-quantum rekeying inside an ECDH ratchet; claims post-quantum forward secrecy and post-compromise security (Level 3 on Apple's own scale), with ECDSA device signatures still classical; rekeying cadence is traded against message size.
bitmessage_link: A production design for post-quantum PCS on an asynchronous channel; the rekey-period trade-off is the bandwidth-versus-healing choice any flooded network must make.

title: Advancing iMessage security: iMessage Contact Key Verification
note: Key transparency for the iMessage key directory: a verifiable log lets devices detect a malicious or compromised directory serving the wrong keys; users get automatic verification plus an out-of-band check; claims detection (not prevention) of key-directory attacks.
bitmessage_link: Bitmessage avoids a key directory by embedding the key hash in the address; the cost is no human-readable names. Key transparency is how directory-based systems close the same trust gap.

title: The Messaging Layer Security (MLS) Protocol
note: Asynchronous group key establishment with a ratchet tree (TreeKEM): O(log n) updates, forward secrecy and post-compromise security for groups, authenticated membership changes via Add/Update/Remove proposals and Commits, epoch-based key schedule; claims confidentiality, integrity, authentication, membership agreement, asynchronicity, PCS; leaves open metadata hiding and concurrency/robustness limits.
bitmessage_link: The group answer Bitmessage lacks: chans there share one passphrase-derived key forever, so membership change means a new key for everyone and no PCS. MLS gives per-epoch keys and cheap add/remove.

title: The Messaging Layer Security (MLS) Architecture
note: Describes the delivery service and authentication service roles around MLS and the security model; states what MLS does not hide (group size, membership, sender identity metadata to the delivery service, message timing) and the trust assumptions on the authentication service.
bitmessage_link: Names the metadata a delivery service sees in a modern group messenger; a useful baseline for what flooding-based designs can improve.

title: Hybrid Public Key Encryption
note: Standard KEM-DEM public-key encryption (DHKEM, KDF, AEAD) with base, PSK, auth modes; used by MLS for TreeKEM node encryption; sender authentication in auth mode but no forward secrecy of the recipient key.
bitmessage_link: Modern replacement for Bitmessage's ECIES to a static recipient key; still static-key, so forward secrecy must come from the surrounding protocol.

title: Terminology for Post-Quantum Traditional Hybrid Schemes
note: Defines PQ/T hybrid terminology (PQ/T hybrid key establishment, composite, non-composite, hybrid signature); no security claims, but fixes vocabulary used by hybrid-KEM and hybrid-signature work in messaging.
bitmessage_link: none direct

title: X-Wing: general-purpose hybrid post-quantum KEM (draft-connolly-cfrg-xwing-kem-11)
venue: IETF Internet-Draft, CFRG, revision 11 (2026-09-23); first draft 2024
note: Specifies X-Wing, a hybrid KEM from X25519 and ML-KEM-768 with a SHA3-256 combiner that exploits ML-KEM's ciphertext binding to avoid hashing the ML-KEM ciphertext; claims IND-CCA security if either component is secure (X-Wing paper proves this).
bitmessage_link: Drop-in hybrid replacement for the classical ECDH step in static-key encryption such as Bitmessage's.

title: Key Transparency Protocol (draft-ietf-keytrans-protocol-05)
venue: IETF Internet-Draft, KEYTRANS WG, revision 05 (2026-07-06); individual-draft predecessor draft-keytrans-mcmillion-protocol (date not checked)
note: Protocol for a third-party-auditable key directory: a prefix tree of versioned keys inside a log; clients get inclusion/non-inclusion proofs, monotonicity and consistency checks; claims users either get the true key bindings or detect interference.
bitmessage_link: Directory-based answer to the binding of names to keys that Bitmessage sidesteps with self-certifying addresses.

title: Key Transparency Architecture (draft-ietf-keytrans-architecture-09)
venue: IETF Internet-Draft, KEYTRANS WG, revision 09 (2026-06-30); individual-draft predecessor draft-mcmillion-keytrans-architecture (date not checked)
note: Terminology, interaction patterns and security properties of Key Transparency in group-messaging deployments; specifies what the protocol guarantees (and what it cannot, e.g. split-view defence needs gossip or third-party auditors).
bitmessage_link: none direct

title: FIPS 203: Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism Standard (ML-KEM)
authors: National Institute of Standards and Technology
note: Standardises ML-KEM-512/768/1024 (IND-CCA2 KEM from module-LWE); the post-quantum KEM used in PQXDH, SPQR, PQ3, X-Wing and MLS PQ ciphersuites; no sender authentication, and encapsulation keys are about 800-1568 bytes.
bitmessage_link: Ciphertext and key sizes matter for Bitmessage-style flooding where every object is replicated to every node.

title: FIPS 204: Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Standard (ML-DSA)
authors: National Institute of Standards and Technology
note: Standardises ML-DSA-44/65/87 (Fiat-Shamir with aborts over module lattices), the main post-quantum signature candidate for messaging identity keys and MLS credentials; signatures are about 2.4-4.6 kB and public keys 1.3-2.6 kB, much larger than Ed25519.
bitmessage_link: Bitmessage signs every object with ECDSA and carries the sender key in the object; ML-DSA signatures are tens of times larger than ECDSA signatures.

title: FIPS 205: Stateless Hash-Based Digital Signature Standard (SLH-DSA)
authors: National Institute of Standards and Technology
note: Standardises SLH-DSA (SPHINCS+), a hash-based stateless signature with conservative assumptions but 8-50 kB signatures; the fallback to lattice assumptions for long-lived identity or root keys.
bitmessage_link: Signature size is prohibitive for per-object signing in a flooded network.

title: Olm: A Cryptographic Ratchet
venue: Matrix libolm specification (docs/olm.md; undated source, converted to markdown 2019-05-14; original year approximate)
note: Matrix's pairwise Double Ratchet variant used for to-device sessions and key sharing; claims forward secrecy and post-compromise security per Double Ratchet; used to distribute Megolm session keys, so it governs group-key delivery.
bitmessage_link: Pairwise ratcheted channel used for key sharing in a federated, store-and-forward system, comparable to Bitmessage's asynchronous delivery but with per-session keys.

title: Megolm group ratchet
venue: Matrix libolm specification (docs/megolm.md; undated source, converted to markdown 2019-05-14; original year approximate)
note: Sender-key style hash ratchet for room messages: one outbound session per sender device, ratchet state shared to members over Olm; the spec lists its own limits: only partial forward secrecy (a recipient keeping an early ratchet value can decrypt everything after it), no backward secrecy / post-compromise security (a compromised session key exposes all later messages until a new session starts), message replay, and no transcript consistency across group members.
bitmessage_link: Closest deployed analogue to a Bitmessage chan: one symmetric group key that never heals. Megolm at least ratchets forward and rotates on member removal.

title: WhatsApp Encryption Overview: Technical white paper (Version 9)
venue: WhatsApp whitepaper, version 1 published 2016-04-05; saved copy is version 9 (2026-02-25)
note: Describes WhatsApp's Signal-protocol sessions, Sender Keys for groups (sender key distributed pairwise, ratcheted per message, rotated on membership removal), multi-device companion model, sender-side backfill and history sync; claims end-to-end confidentiality with forward secrecy; does not claim post-compromise security for groups or hide metadata from the server.
bitmessage_link: Largest deployment of the sender-key group model; membership privacy and metadata are in server hands, where Bitmessage hid recipients by flooding.

title: mpENC Multi-Party Encrypted Messaging Protocol design document
note: Design document (Mega, January 2016) for multi-party encrypted messaging: a session model with membership, message order, authorship and readers; discusses authenticity and confidentiality of each category (including authentication of membership changes, which message signing alone does not give), group key agreement, and reliability and consistency among members over untrusted servers.
bitmessage_link: An early (2015-16) group chat design over untrusted store-and-forward servers, close in setting to Bitmessage chans but with membership-aware keys.

title: SoK: Secure Messaging
note: Systematises secure messaging along trust establishment, conversation security (forward secrecy, future secrecy, deniability, participant consistency, speaker consistency, causality preservation, asynchronicity) and transport privacy; rates dozens of messaging systems and transport schemes; discusses Bitmessage only as a broadcast-based transport (broadcast gives recipient anonymity and unlinkability against network attackers but needs high bandwidth, has no asynchronicity support and scales badly; Bitmessage limits spam with proof of work or fees, adding computation and delay, the blockchains row of its transport table); the baseline taxonomy for later work.
bitmessage_link: Cites Bitmessage as the broadcast-transport example and defines the properties (forward secrecy, future secrecy, participant consistency, asynchronicity) that static-key encryption lacks.

title: SoK: Secure Messaging (University of Waterloo technical report CACR 2015-02)
venue: Waterloo CACR technical report 2015-02 (extended version with full system tables)
note: Extended technical-report version of the S&P 2015 SoK with fuller per-system tables and discussion (OTR, mpOTR, TextSecure, Pond, Cryptocat and others; Bitmessage again as the broadcast-based transport example); same property taxonomy.
bitmessage_link: Extended justification for the broadcast-transport trade-offs that apply to Bitmessage.

title: Improving Signal's Sealed Sender
note: Shows sealed sender's one-sided sender anonymity does not compose over a conversation: a statistical disclosure attack using default delivery receipts links users in as few as 5 messages, even for Tor/VPN users; presents mitigations with a simulation-based proof of one-sided anonymity (simplest reuses existing sealed-sender mechanisms; the strongest costs under 40 USD per month for millions of users).
bitmessage_link: Confirms that hiding the sender in the envelope is not enough against timing; Bitmessage's flooding avoids recipient correlation but exposes network-level sender timing (Dandelion was added later).

title: No safety in numbers: traffic analysis of sealed-sender groups in Signal (poster)
note: Extends the Martiny et al. statistical disclosure attack on sealed sender from communicating pairs to whole group conversations (three or more users on one channel), using the server-visible record of who receives messages; shows sealed sender does not hide group senders from a delivery-observing server.
bitmessage_link: Group fan-out is where server-side metadata leaks; broadcast flooding hides group structure but at O(N) bandwidth.

title: Four Attacks and a Proof for Telegram
note: Analyses MTProto 2.0 symmetric channel: four attacks (reordering across directions, ciphertext-integrity gaps, a timing side channel, a plaintext-recovery attack against the IGE mode) and a proof of security of a modified protocol; relevant as a warning that custom session protocols without formal analysis break.
bitmessage_link: Another non-standard messenger protocol that needed independent cryptanalysis; Bitmessage's own encryption was never formally analysed.

title: Automated Verification for Secure Messaging Protocols and their Implementations: A Symbolic and Computational Approach
note: Method (ProScript code translated to ProVerif and CryptoVerif models) applied to a variant of the Signal protocol (X3DH plus Double Ratchet, as shipped in Cryptocat); finds new and previously known weaknesses in the protocol under a range of threat models (compromise of long-term and session keys) and suggests countermeasures; targets confidentiality, authentication, forward and future secrecy.
bitmessage_link: Method template for formally checking session protocols; no equivalent exists for Bitmessage.

title: Formal verification of the PQXDH Post-Quantum key agreement protocol for end-to-end secure messaging
note: Formal specification and ProVerif/CryptoVerif analysis of PQXDH asking whether it keeps X3DH's guarantees, gives post-quantum forward secrecy and can run alongside X3DH; finds several flaws and potential vulnerabilities in the specification (not exploitable in the Signal app because of implementation choices), identifies a needed KEM binding property (formally defined and proved for Kyber), and yields a corrected specification with proofs.
bitmessage_link: Shows what a verified post-quantum upgrade of a handshake requires; Bitmessage has no handshake.

title: Formal Models and Verified Protocols for Group Messaging: Attacks and Proofs for IETF MLS
note: Formal framework in F* comparing candidate MLS protocols up to draft 7; executable specification and symbolic proof of TreeKEM_B (draft-7 group key establishment) handling unbounded groups and fine-grained compromise; finds new attacks and proposes verified fixes adopted into MLS; first mechanically checked proof for MLS.
bitmessage_link: Group-state authentication is the property Bitmessage chans have by construction only through a shared secret; MLS must prove it for dynamic membership.

title: TreeKEM: Asynchronous Decentralized Key Management for Large Dynamic Groups (A protocol proposal for Messaging Layer Security)
note: Original TreeKEM proposal: ratchet tree of DH/KEM keys giving O(log n) group key updates with forward secrecy and post-compromise security; claims asynchronous, decentralised membership operations with healing after each member's update.
bitmessage_link: Replaces Bitmessage's chan passphrase model with logarithmic-cost rekeying.

title: The Complexities of Healing in Secure Group Messaging: Why Cross-Group Effects Matter
note: First analysis of healing when a user is in several groups: group-key designs (ART, TreeKEM, MLS draft 11) give much weaker post-compromise security than pairwise-channel group designs, and never fully heal authentication if new users can be created dynamically; proposes global updates plus post-compromise-secure signatures, with a security definition and instantiation.
bitmessage_link: Bitmessage identities reused across chans are the analogue: one compromised key exposes every group it belongs to.

title: Three Lessons From Threema: Analysis of a Secure Messenger
note: Seven attacks on Threema in three threat models (external actor, compromised server, compelled access), including undetectable reordering and deletion of messages through nonce handling, replay and reflection, ephemeral client-to-server key compromise, and a 'Kompromat' attack letting a server create incriminating messages; Threema lacked fine-grained forward secrecy and post-compromise security; all patched; draws lessons for protocol designers.
bitmessage_link: Static long-term keys without ratcheting are exactly Threema's pre-fix design; a worked example of what breaks.

title: Improved Strongly Deniable Authenticated Key Exchanges for Secure Messaging
note: Constructs deniable AKEs (Spawn, Spawn-Dual, Spawn-Dual-Quick) that give strong deniability (even against an online judge) with forward secrecy and KCI resistance, usable as OTR/Signal-like handshakes; includes comparison of deniability notions.
bitmessage_link: Bitmessage messages are signed by the sender and therefore non-repudiable; deniable AKE is the alternative.

title: TreeKEM: A Modular Machine-Checked Symbolic Security Analysis of Group Key Agreement in Messaging Layer Security
note: Machine-checked symbolic analysis of RFC 9420 TreeKEM that models the precise protocol (not an abstraction) and proves confidentiality, forward secrecy and post-compromise security with respect to bounded compromise, in a modular way (TreeSync, TreeKEM, TreeDEM).
bitmessage_link: Group-key assurance level that chan-style shared secrets cannot reach.

title: Formal Verification of a Post-Quantum Signal Protocol with Tamarin
note: Tamarin model of a post-quantum variant of Signal (PQ handshake and ratchet) checking secrecy, forward secrecy and post-compromise security against a Dolev-Yao adversary with KEM-based replacements; reports no attacks in the modelled variant.
bitmessage_link: none direct

title: A Verification Framework for Secure Group Messaging
note: Thesis covering the verified specification and implementation of MLS components (TreeSync authenticated group state, TreeKEM symbolic analysis, DY* framework); summarises the properties proved: group-state agreement, confidentiality, forward secrecy, PCS.
bitmessage_link: none direct

title: Security and Efficiency of Secure Group Messaging Protocols
note: Thesis on CGKA/MLS: quarantined handling of inactive members (Quarantined-TreeKEM), tree-shaping to lower communication cost (Bonsai), security-efficiency trade-offs of PCS for groups.
bitmessage_link: none direct

title: On the security of instant messaging: towards solutions for multi-device and group applications
venue: PhD thesis, Université de Rennes / Orange Labs (hal tel-03592828)
note: Thesis on reaching optimal security (forward secrecy, post-compromise security) in multi-device and group messaging, including 'Multi-Device for Signal' and group extensions with efficiency analysis.
bitmessage_link: none direct

title: NEXTLEAP: Decentralizing Identity with Privacy for Secure Messaging
note: Project paper describing privacy-preserving federated identity, verified key directories (CONIKS-style) and metadata-protecting messaging (Panoramix mix network) as a decentralised alternative to centralised key servers.
bitmessage_link: Attempts to solve the same decentralised-identity-and-metadata problem Bitmessage addressed, with key verification and a mixnet instead of flooding.

title: Bots can Snoop: Uncovering and Mitigating Privacy Risks of Bots in Group Chats
note: Finds chatbots in group chats read far more messages than needed and can link a user across groups (3.6 percent chance on joining a new group with bots); proposes SnoopGuard on top of MLS giving selective message access and sender anonymity toward bots at O(log n + m) sending cost.
bitmessage_link: none direct

title: DKVE: Decentralized Key Validation for End-to-End Encrypted Messaging
note: Validates a contact's public key by cross-checking with mutual contacts in the social graph (OPRF and oblivious key-value stores to keep queries and contact lists private; sequential probability ratio test to detect server misbehaviour); simulations detect man-in-the-middle attacks above 97 percent for strong-to-moderate-tie networks; complements, does not replace, key transparency and out-of-band checks.
bitmessage_link: Decentralised key validation addresses the key-binding problem Bitmessage avoids with self-certifying addresses, at the price of unreadable names.

title: Send and Pretend: Exploiting Transcript Consistency Issues in End-to-End Encrypted Group Chats
note: Shows that WhatsApp, Signal, iMessage, Threema and others guarantee no transcript consistency in group chats: a malicious member can selectively omit, reorder or alter content per recipient (via fallback paths or pairwise channels inside groups) without UI warnings, e.g. to rig polls; outlines low-overhead mitigations and UI signalling.
bitmessage_link: Participant/transcript consistency is a property store-and-forward flooding gives no help with; Bitmessage chans have no consistency guarantee either.

title: Off-the-Record Communication, or, Why Not To Use PGP
note: Introduced OTR: ephemeral DH with rekeying for forward secrecy, MAC key publication for deniability (malleable encryption), authentication without non-repudiation; the ancestor of the Signal ratchet and the deniability goal.
bitmessage_link: Bitmessage's signed objects are the opposite of OTR's deniability goal; OTR is the 2004 baseline for forward secrecy and deniability.

title: Multi-party Off-the-Record Messaging
note: Group OTR: authenticated group key agreement, deniable authentication within the group, forward secrecy, and participant/transcript consistency; designed for synchronous multi-party chat.
bitmessage_link: The group-chat deniability and consistency baseline that Bitmessage chans (shared key, signed messages) do not offer.

title: Messenger Secret Conversations: Technical Whitepaper
venue: Facebook whitepaper, version 1.0 2016-07-08; saved copy is version 2.0 (2017-05-18)
note: Describes Messenger's opt-in end-to-end 'secret conversations' built on the Signal Protocol (prekeys, ratcheted keys, per-device sessions; conversations with more than two devices use the Signal group messaging protocol, i.e. sender keys), with a message franking mechanism for abuse reports that must satisfy authenticity, confidentiality and third-party deniability; claims content confidentiality and forward secrecy through the hash ratchet; metadata stays with the server.
bitmessage_link: Large-scale deployment of the pairwise-session model that Bitmessage lacks; also introduces abuse reporting over E2EE, the counterpart of Bitmessage's proof-of-work anti-spam.

title: Messenger End-to-End Encryption Overview
note: Messenger's default E2EE design: Signal Protocol sessions, group messages with Sender Keys over server-side fan-out, device registration, and a new server-side storage protocol for message history; claims content confidentiality and forward secrecy through hash ratchets for 1:1 and group sessions; the server still sees who communicates and when.
bitmessage_link: Shows how a large service layers storage and history restore on a ratcheted pairwise design, the property trade-off Bitmessage's network-wide object retention embodies.

title: Wire Security Whitepaper
venue: Wire whitepaper, saved copy dated 2021-07-19 (earlier versions exist; earliest date not checked)
note: Specifies Wire's Proteus protocol (an independent implementation of the Axolotl/Double Ratchet with prekeys and a last-resort prekey, using Curve25519, ChaCha20, HMAC-SHA256 and HKDF), end-to-end encryption between pairs of clients (up to 8 clients per user, conversations synchronised across devices), client registration, and a legal hold service that stores conversation content on a compliance server; relies on the ratchet for forward secrecy and healing (no separate claims beyond the Double Ratchet's).
bitmessage_link: Pairwise-session model (one ratchet per client pair) versus Bitmessage's single static key per address; legal hold shows the compliance pressure on E2EE designs.

title: Recommendations for Key-Encapsulation Mechanisms (NIST SP 800-227)
note: NIST guidance on using KEMs (including ML-KEM): security properties (IND-CCA), key-derivation and combiner requirements, and rules for hybrid constructions mixing classical and post-quantum shared secrets.
bitmessage_link: Reference rules for upgrading a classical ECDH step to a hybrid KEM combiner.

title: Transparency Dictionaries with Succinct Proofs of Correct Operation
note: Verdict: a transparency dictionary (untrusted service keeps a label-value map used for end-to-end-encryption key lookup) that proves publicly verifiably that every read and authorised update was executed correctly; composes indexed Merkle trees (SNARK-friendly) with the Phalanx SNARK for amortised constant-size proofs; scales to millions of labels with modest overhead.
bitmessage_link: Directory-auditing building block; Bitmessage avoids a directory by self-certifying addresses.

title: End-to-End Encrypted Messaging Protocols: An Overview
note: Overview and comparison of end-to-end encrypted messaging protocols and applications (Signal, OTR, OpenPGP-based and others) with discussion of their security properties and usability; a survey that complements Unger et al.'s SoK. (Metadata only: no open copy located.) (No open full text retrieved: meta.)
bitmessage_link: Survey context placing decentralised messengers among E2EE protocols.

title: Hybrid Key Exchange in TLS 1.3
venue: IETF RFC 9954 (July 2026); individual draft draft-ietf-tls-hybrid-design since 2019
note: Design of hybrid key exchange (concatenate shared secrets from several key-exchange algorithms and feed them into the key schedule) so security holds if any component holds; gives the combiner rules (concatenation, ordering, security considerations) reused by hybrid messaging handshakes.
bitmessage_link: none direct

title: Post-Quantum Traditional (PQ/T) Hybrid Key Agreement Mechanisms for TLS 1.3
note: Standards-track hybrid key agreements for TLS 1.3 combining ECDHE (X25519, secp256r1/384r1) with ML-KEM (e.g. X25519MLKEM768); concretises the hybrid combiner with FIPS 203 KEMs; IND-CCA security if either component holds.
bitmessage_link: none direct

title: Amortized PQ MLS Combiner (draft-ietf-mls-combiner-02)
venue: IETF Internet-Draft, MLS WG, revision 02 (2025-10-20), now expired
note: Combines a traditional MLS session with a post-quantum MLS session by seeding the exporter secret of the PQ session into the traditional one; supports cheap traditional-only (PARTIAL) and hybrid PQ (FULL) key updates so that PQ KEM and signature cost is amortised while keeping frequent key rotation; targets amortised PQ confidentiality and authenticity.
bitmessage_link: Shows how to pay the post-quantum bandwidth cost only occasionally in a group session.

title: Deniable Authentication and Key Exchange
note: Extends Dwork-Naor-Sahai deniable authentication to deniable key exchange and proves deniability of SKEME (full deniability from plaintext awareness of the encryption) and SIGMA (the basis of IKE); the definitions later used to analyse X3DH, PQXDH and post-quantum Signal handshakes. (Metadata only: ePrint offers a PostScript file only, https://eprint.iacr.org/2006/280.ps.) (No open full text retrieved: only a PostScript copy is open.)
bitmessage_link: Defines the deniability notion that signed Bitmessage objects (non-repudiable sender signatures) do not satisfy.

title: A Formal Security Analysis of the Signal Messaging Protocol
note: First formal security analysis of Signal's X3DH plus Double Ratchet as a multi-stage key exchange with a tree of stages; proves key indistinguishability, forward secrecy and post-compromise ('future') secrecy for the key-exchange core under stated assumptions and finds no major flaw; does not model message encryption, deniability or the server.
bitmessage_link: The reference model for what Bitmessage's static-key encryption lacks: forward secrecy and healing from key compromise.

title: The Double Ratchet: Security Notions, Proofs, and Modularization for the Signal Protocol
note: Defines secure messaging (SM) security with fine-grained state compromise and proves the Double Ratchet secure by splitting it into continuous key agreement (CKA), forward-secure AEAD and a PRF-PRNG; shows the combination of forward security, post-compromise security and immediate (no-delay) decryption; identifies the three-component modularisation that later work (SPQR, Triple Ratchet) reuses.
bitmessage_link: Gives the proof-level definition of the properties (forward security, PCS, immediate decryption) that a flooded static-key design does not claim.

title: Ratcheted Encryption and Key Exchange: The Security of Messaging
note: Defines syntax and security for ratcheted encryption and key exchange (formalising the key-ratcheting idea of Borisov, Goldberg and Brewer, extended in messengers); gives a proven-secure ratcheted key exchange and a generic way to get ratcheted encryption from it plus standard encryption; model restricted to unidirectional communication and exposure of one party (later extended by Poettering-Rosler).
bitmessage_link: Formalises why a static key (as in Bitmessage) cannot meet forward or backward secrecy.

title: Asynchronous ratcheted key exchange
note: Develops strong security definitions for ratcheted key exchange (RKE), both unidirectional and where both parties contribute, with full state exposure of either party (the earlier Bellare et al. model was restricted to unidirectional communication and exposure of one party); shows that optimal security needs key-updatable cryptographic primitives and builds the protocol from a key-updatable KEM (itself obtained from HIBE-style techniques); gives forward secrecy and post-compromise security in the asynchronous bidirectional setting.
bitmessage_link: Shows the primitive-level cost (key-updatable KEMs) of strong asynchronous session security.

title: Optimal Channel Security Against Fine-Grained State Compromise: The Safety of Messaging
note: Defines the best possible security of a bidirectional channel against repeated fine-grained state compromise and gives a proven-secure construction (with updatable public-key encryption and signatures) that is strictly stronger than the Double Ratchet; showing that the Double Ratchet is not optimal and at what cost optimal security can be had.
bitmessage_link: Provides the upper bound against which static-key and ratchet designs can be compared.

title: Efficient Ratcheting: Almost-Optimal Guarantees for Secure Messaging
note: Almost-optimal security notion for secure messaging that tolerates exposure of secret state and local randomness (forward secrecy, backward secrecy / healing, immediate decryption), with constructions far more efficient than the optimal-security constructions of Jaeger-Stepanovs and Poettering-Rosler (which pay an extreme efficiency loss compared with Signal) while closing most of the gap to Signal's guarantees.
bitmessage_link: Quantifies the efficiency of stronger-than-Signal session security, relevant to the per-message bandwidth cost of any flooded network.

title: Bidirectional Asynchronous Ratcheted Key Agreement with Linear Complexity
note: Defines bidirectional asynchronous ratcheted key agreement (BARK) with formal security notions and gives a scheme with O(n) complexity for n messages, using no key-update primitives and no random oracle (earlier bidirectional schemes needed heavy key-update primitives, random oracles and O(n^2) complexity); built from a cryptosystem, a signature scheme and a one-time signature; forward secrecy and post-compromise security with 0-RTT.
bitmessage_link: none direct

title: On the Tight Security of the Double Ratchet
note: Tight security bounds for the Double Ratchet in the multi-session setting, revisiting the Alwen-Coretti-Dodis modular decomposition; prior proofs gave guarantees that degrade with the number of interactions even in the single-session case; covers forward security, post-compromise security, adaptive state corruption, injections and out-of-order delivery.
bitmessage_link: none direct

title: Triple Ratchet: A Bandwidth Efficient Hybrid-Secure Signal Protocol
note: Gives a hybrid-secure Signal protocol (Triple Ratchet) that runs a post-quantum sparse continuous key agreement (ML-KEM with erasure codes) next to the classical Double Ratchet and mixes the outputs, achieving forward secrecy and post-compromise security against quantum adversaries while keeping per-message bandwidth close to the classical ratchet; formal model and proof of hybrid security; basis of Signal's SPQR.
bitmessage_link: Establishes the bandwidth floor of post-quantum PCS, an essential cost for flooded networks.

title: Security of Symmetric Ratchets and Key Chains - Implications for Protocols like TLS 1.3, Signal, and PQ3
note: Analyses one-way key chains and symmetric ratchets (TLS 1.3, Signal, MLS, PQ3): the hash-chain construction used by Signal and PQ3 has weak keys and an unexpectedly high rate of key collisions after many steps (security degrades with chain length), while other constructions do not; recommends constructions and chain-length limits.
bitmessage_link: Relevant to any design that derives per-message keys by hashing a chain; chain length and skipped keys are exposed in store-and-forward delivery.

title: ASMesh: Anonymous and Secure Messaging in Mesh Networks Using Stronger, Anonymous Double Ratchet
note: Messaging for mesh networks (no central relay; clients relay ciphertexts, for scenarios such as mass protests in censored networks): a new security model capturing forward and post-compromise security as well as forward and post-compromise anonymity, stronger confidentiality goals possible because of delay and distribution, and ASMesh, a provably secure protocol built on a stronger anonymous Double Ratchet; motivated by attacks on deployed mesh messengers.
bitmessage_link: A direct successor of Bitmessage's setting (untrusted relays, no server) that adds a ratchet and unlinkable headers.

title: Strongly Anonymous Ratcheted Key Exchange
note: Defines anonymity (hiding metadata about participants) for ratcheted key exchange under continuous, temporary exposure of user secrets, the first use of RKE to obtain strong anonymity guarantees under such exposure, and gives a strongly anonymous RKE construction alongside forward secrecy and post-compromise security.
bitmessage_link: Closest theory to merging Bitmessage-style recipient privacy (key privacy, trial decryption) with ratcheted session keys.

title: GURKE: Group Unidirectional Ratcheted Key Exchange
note: Group unidirectional ratcheted key exchange: restricts CGKA so that members are either senders or receivers (a sender group Alice establishes keys to a receiver group Bob), giving forward security and post-compromise security for the sender side and forward security for receivers, with constructions simpler and cheaper than full CGKA.
bitmessage_link: One-to-many ratcheting matches the Bitmessage broadcast/subscription pattern, where one sender writes to many readers.

title: Towards Leakage-Resilient Ratcheted Key Exchange
note: Formalises a key-indistinguishability game for unidirectional ratcheted key exchange (one sender, one receiver) with partial leakage of party state rather than only full state exposure, building on Balli-Rosler-Vaudenay, with constructions that keep forward security and post-compromise security under bounded leakage.
bitmessage_link: none direct

title: RHQC: post-quantum ratcheted key exchange from coding assumptions
note: Turns the HQC code-based cryptosystem into a ratcheted key exchange, giving a first code-based RKE with perfect forward secrecy and post-compromise security as a non-lattice alternative to ML-KEM ratchets.
bitmessage_link: none direct

title: MARSHAL: Messaging with Asynchronous Ratchets and Signatures for faster HeALing
note: Improves Signal's healing: Signal needs up to two full message chains to recover after compromise; MARSHAL (asynchronous ratchets plus signatures) recovers after about one chain while keeping forward secrecy.
bitmessage_link: none direct

title: Automated formal analysis of Signal’s Double Ratchet: attacks, fixes and security proofs
note: First formal analysis of the Double Ratchet that covers all features (including out-of-order arrivals), highly automated, over all key compromises, and proves post-compromise security (PCS); partial results for header-encrypted and PQ-extended variants; reports attacks on earlier or alternative versions and fixes.
bitmessage_link: none direct

title: Anamorphic Messaging: Analyzing the Double Ratchet, Triple Ratchet, PQ3, and MLS
note: Shows how anamorphic (hidden double-key) messages can be embedded in the Double Ratchet, Triple Ratchet, PQ3 and MLS randomness and key material, so a user forced to surrender keys can still convey hidden messages; analyses what each ratchet design leaves as embeddable spots.
bitmessage_link: Coercion-resistance angle: a hidden channel under key-surrender duress; relevant to deniability and plausible deniability threat models.

title: Secrecy in Squirrel and the Post-Compromise Security of a Ratchet
note: First mechanised computational-model proof of a ratchet's post-compromise security (using the Squirrel prover), covering a Signal-style ratchet; shows secrecy of session keys under state compromise with healing.
bitmessage_link: none direct

title: Towards Post-Quantum Security for Signal's X3DH Handshake
note: Introduces split KEMs, which translate the key reusability of a DH-based protocol to a KEM-based flow, and lifts Signal's X3DH handshake to the post-quantum KEM setting without additional message flows; gives security notions for split KEMs and shows most post-quantum KEMs (lattice, isogeny) are not secure under key reuse, which is why a plain KEM drop-in for DH fails.
bitmessage_link: Argues that long-lived static recipient keys (as in Bitmessage addresses) are the hardest case for post-quantum migration because lattice KEMs tolerate key reuse only with CCA security.

title: An Efficient and Generic Construction for Signal's Handshake (X3DH): Post-Quantum, State Leakage Secure, and Deniable
note: Casts X3DH as a 'Signal-conforming' authenticated key exchange with a formal security model (including leakage of state) and gives the first efficient generic construction from standard primitives such as KEMs and signature schemes, instantiable post-quantum, with state-leakage resilience and a form of deniability.
bitmessage_link: none direct

title: Post-quantum Asynchronous Deniable Key Exchange and the Signal Handshake
note: Builds post-quantum asynchronous deniable key exchange from KEMs combined with designated-verifier signatures (with candidate post-quantum DVS schemes), because no plain KEM replacement for the Signal handshake achieves asynchrony, implicit mutual authentication with deniability, and security under key compromise; proves forward secrecy and deniability.
bitmessage_link: Bitmessage signs every message with the sender key and so gives no deniability; this line shows deniability is preserved post-quantum only with extra cost.

title: On the Cryptographic Deniability of the Signal Protocol
note: First formal study of offline deniability of the Signal protocol: building a deniability proof is non-trivial and needs strong assumptions (e.g. knowledge-type assumptions on groups); analyses implicitly authenticated key exchanges (X3DH, 3DH, HMQV-style) and proves deniability under those assumptions.
bitmessage_link: Sets the standard for what 'deniable' means for X3DH; Bitmessage objects are signed and thus non-deniable.

title: A Deniability Analysis of Signal's Initial Handshake PQXDH
note: Shows PQXDH does not meet X3DH's deniability because of the signature on the ephemeral key; analysis relies on plaintext awareness of the KEM, which Signal's PQXDH implementation does not provide; initiator and responder get different deniability guarantees due to protocol asymmetry; introduces a finer-grained deniability model (including malicious adversaries in the big-brother model).
bitmessage_link: none direct

title: K-Waay: Fast and Deniable Post-Quantum X3DH without Ring Signatures
note: Fast deniable post-quantum X3DH that replaces ring signatures with a new 'split KEM' used for authentication; claims asynchrony, post-quantum security and deniability (in the sense of Brendel et al.) with much smaller message sizes than ring-signature constructions.
bitmessage_link: none direct

title: Practical Deniable Post-Quantum X3DH: A Lightweight Split-KEM for K-Waay
note: Sparrow-KEM and Sym-Sparrow-KEM: lightweight split KEMs that shrink K-Waay (post-quantum deniable X3DH) to sizes competitive with ring-signature designs, with a 40x speedup; Sym-Sparrow-KEM is the first symmetric split KEM offering deniability, IND-1KCA and IND-1BatchCCA security; keeps asynchrony and deniability.
bitmessage_link: none direct

title: Comprehensive Deniability Analysis of Signal Handshake Protocols: X3DH, PQXDH to Fully Post-Quantum with Deniable Ring Signatures
note: Unified deniability framework for Signal handshake protocols; shows X3DH deniability holds under a clean AKE definition, finds PQXDH's classical authentication weakens it, and builds a fully post-quantum handshake with deniable ring signatures; compares all prior notions.
bitmessage_link: none direct

title: Shadowfax: Hybrid Security and Deniability for AKEMs
note: Shadowfax: hybrid-secure authenticated KEM that combines a classical non-interactive key exchange, a post-quantum KEM and a post-quantum ring signature to preserve deniability (which X3DH has but PQXDH and PQ3 lose) while keeping hybrid confidentiality; deniability in both dishonest and honest settings.
bitmessage_link: none direct

title: Real-World Deniability in Messaging
note: Model of real-world deniability that covers the whole messaging system (not only the cryptographic protocol); concludes Signal and DKIM-signed email give no practical deniability; also finds, in 140 Swiss court cases, that no judgment considered deniability.
bitmessage_link: Bitmessage's non-repudiable signatures are the extreme case; this paper argues even 'deniable' protocols give little practical deniability.

title: X3DH with Deniable Authentication without Trusted Third Parties
note: Extends X3DH to message authentication in the short-authenticated-string model (no trusted third party) using a VRF-based SAS scheme on ephemeral keys, keeping deniability and adding authentication without a PKI.
bitmessage_link: Decentralised, directory-free authentication in the style of Bitmessage's out-of-band address exchange.

title: NOTRY: deniable messaging with retroactive avowal
note: NOTRY: deniable messaging where users can retroactively avow a conversation transcript (avowable designated-verifier proofs), at about 8x communication and computation overhead.
bitmessage_link: none direct

title: Post-Compromise Security
note: Introduces post-compromise security (PCS): security can be restored after a party's long-term secrets are compromised, under conditions (the adversary must be passive for a time); gives first informal and formal definitions in AKE and two strong security models; shows PCS requires the attacker to stop interfering and that protocols with ratcheting can achieve it.
bitmessage_link: Names the property Bitmessage's static key can never achieve: once the key is stolen, all future messages are exposed.

title: On Ends-to-Ends Encryption: Asynchronous Group Messaging with Strong Security Guarantees
note: Asynchronous Ratcheting Trees (ART): tree-based group key exchange in which no two parties ever need to be online at once, giving logarithmic-cost updates, forward secrecy and post-compromise security for groups; observes that deployed group messengers silently give groups a weaker property (an adversary who compromises one member can intercept communications indefinitely); includes a computational security proof for ART's core.
bitmessage_link: Group-level counterpart of the Double Ratchet; the Bitmessage chan has none of these properties (a shared passphrase forever).

title: Security Analysis and Improvements for the IETF MLS Standard for Group Messaging
note: Formal analysis of TreeKEM as a continuous group key agreement (CGKA) protocol: shows TreeKEM achieves post-compromise security in isolation (and slightly more) but that the then-current design does not provide adequate forward secrecy; proposes a modification (inspired by Jost et al. and an idea of Kohbrok) and proves the modified protocol meets stronger security; introduces CGKA as a primitive.
bitmessage_link: Defines the group-key properties missing in chan-style shared keys.

title: Modular Design of Secure Group Messaging Protocols and the Security of MLS
note: Modular framework for secure group messaging (CGKA, forward-secure group AEAD, PRF-PRNG), proves the MLS design secure in the composition, with an adaptive, active adversary and formal treatment of MLS's structure; the modularisation underpins MLS formal reasoning.
bitmessage_link: none direct

title: On The Insider Security of MLS
note: First notion of insider security for CGKA and group messaging (malicious members that adaptively use the PKI, deviate from the protocol and leak states), an Insider Secure TreeKEM (ITK) abstraction of MLS Draft 12 with a rigorous proof, three practical attacks on MLS with fixes now adopted in the standard, and a second attack on MLS-like CGKAs proven secure under earlier notions.
bitmessage_link: Insiders are the dominant threat in chan-like groups where any member holds the shared key.

title: Continuous Group Key Agreement with Active Security
note: Studies CGKA as a stand-alone primitive and presents three new security notions of increasing strength: even the weakest (passive) notion already admits attacks on all prior constructions (including all TreeKEM variants), and the two active notions let the adversary use exposed states and full network control (related to insider attacks), with the first meaningful post-compromise and forward secrecy guarantees (PCFS) against such adversaries and the first composable notions; gives constructions.
bitmessage_link: none direct

title: Cryptographic Security of the MLS RFC, Draft 11
note: Studies the MLS continuous group key distribution (key schedule, TreeKEM and their composition) as specified in Draft 11, abstracting away signatures, message flow and authentication; establishes uniqueness and key indistinguishability of epoch keys in the computational model under strong corruption, including post-compromise security.
bitmessage_link: none direct

title: TreeSync: Authenticated Group Management for Messaging Layer Security
note: Formalises TreeSync, MLS's group-integrity and authentication layer (authenticated tree of members and keys); gives a verified F* implementation and proves that group members agree on the tree and that only authorised members change it; identifies flaws in early drafts' state authentication.
bitmessage_link: Membership integrity and authenticated group state are exactly what chan passphrases do not provide.

title: Fork-Resilient Continuous Group Key Agreement
note: Defines fork-resilient CGKA: after the group state forks (diverging histories from server or network failures), members can re-merge safely; shows MLS-like protocols cannot recover safely and proposes a fork-resilient construction using key-update and commit structure.
bitmessage_link: Decentralised/unreliable delivery causes forks; a Bitmessage-style flood network inherits that problem.

title: How to Hide MetaData in MLS-Like Secure Group Messaging: Simple, Modular, and Post-Quantum
note: Generic wrapper turning any CGKA into a metadata-hiding CGKA: uses the continuously evolving shared group key to run an anonymous group-membership authentication towards the server (needs only a standard signature scheme), hiding who is in the group and who communicates, with modest overhead; the wrapper is post-quantum compatible when the CGKA and signature are.
bitmessage_link: Direct answer to the Bitmessage question 'who can see membership and sender' in a group: shows metadata-hiding group key agreement is possible with logarithmic cost.

title: Grafting Key Trees: Efficient Key Management for Overlapping Groups
note: Grafting key trees for overlapping groups: shared sub-trees reduce the bandwidth cost of keeping multiple groups' keys fresh; relevant to users in several groups (the cross-group effects problem).
bitmessage_link: Users in several chans share a key per chan; grafting lowers per-group cost.

title: WhatsUpp with Sender Keys? Analysis, Improvements and Security Proofs
note: First formal analysis of the Sender Keys protocol (used by WhatsApp and Signal groups): new security model for Sender Keys-like protocols integrating two-party messaging, proof of a form of forward secrecy, identification of shortcomings (notably the lack of post-compromise security) and a practical improved protocol with proofs.
bitmessage_link: Sender Keys is the deployed model closest to a chan: one symmetric key per sender and no healing.

title: Practically-exploitable Cryptographic Vulnerabilities in Matrix
note: Practically exploitable cryptographic vulnerabilities in Matrix and Element that, together, invalidate the confidentiality and authentication guarantees claimed against a malicious server; the flaws are insecure design, protocol confusion, lack of domain separation and implementation bugs across the sub-protocols (device verification, key sharing and backup, Megolm session handling) and libraries; all responsibly disclosed; calls for formal analysis.
bitmessage_link: A federated store-and-forward messenger of the same species as Bitmessage; the attacks show what goes wrong when group keys and device lists are managed ad hoc.

title: More is Less: On the End-to-End Security of Group Chats in Signal, WhatsApp, and Threema
note: Security and reliability model for group instant messaging and analysis of Signal, WhatsApp and Threema group chats (their group protocols are described from reverse engineering, since mostly undocumented); finds attacks, including that a malicious server can add members to WhatsApp groups, that removed or malicious members can retain or gain capabilities, and weak guarantees on ordering, forward and backward secrecy for groups; gives countermeasures.
bitmessage_link: Shows that group membership and key management by a server is the weak point; Bitmessage chans avoid a server but have no membership control at all.

title: On the Price of Concurrency in Group Ratcheting Protocols
note: Group ratcheting price of concurrency: pairwise two-party ratchets in parallel give excellent PCS but cost O(n) per message; MLS-style protocols cost O(log n) but forbid concurrent sending and recovery, delaying PCS by up to n communication time steps; the paper analyses this trade-off between communication overhead and concurrency for post-compromise security in groups.
bitmessage_link: Offline, concurrent writers (the Bitmessage setting) are exactly where this impossibility bites.

title: Key Agreement for Decentralized Secure Group Messaging with Strong Security Guarantees
note: Adapts secure group messaging to decentralised networks with no central authority: defines decentralised continuous group key agreement (DCGKA), gives a practical construction with security proof and shows how to build a full messaging protocol from it; forward secrecy and post-compromise security under device compromise, tolerant of offline members and concurrent membership changes; prototype evaluated.
bitmessage_link: A decentralised group-security design with no server, the missing counterpart to Bitmessage's group story.

title: On the Worst-Case Inefficiency of CGKA
note: Negative results on worst-case efficiency of CGKA: shows that CGKA protocols with PCS cannot be efficient (sublinear in group size) in the worst case, only on natural operation sequences, a formal gap behind MLS's O(log n) best case.
bitmessage_link: Limits on how cheaply group keys can be rotated apply to chan-style flooded groups.

title: Keep the Dirt: Tainted TreeKEM, Adaptively and Actively Secure Continuous Group Key Agreement
note: Tainted TreeKEM (TTKEM): a TreeKEM variant more efficient than TreeKEM on natural group-operation distributions (shown by simulation), with two security proofs establishing post-compromise and forward secrecy even against adaptive, active attackers with a security loss quantified in group size and number of operations.
bitmessage_link: none direct

title: A Concrete Treatment of Efficient Continuous Group Key Agreement via Multi-Recipient PKEs
note: Chained CmPKE: a CGKA with an asymmetric bandwidth profile (small commit upload, receivers download more) based on multi-recipient PKE; post-quantum primitives tailored to it cut the growth rate of uploaded commit messages by two or three orders of magnitude; security proof included.
bitmessage_link: none direct

title: Server-Aided Continuous Group Key Agreement
note: Server-aided CGKA (saCGKA): lets the untrusted delivery server do work in the CGKA, giving a modification of ITK (the CGKA underlying MLS) with greatly reduced communication and computation in practice at the same security; the server learns no keys.
bitmessage_link: none direct

title: CoCoA: Concurrent Continuous Group Key Agreement
note: CoCoA: concurrent CGKA in which many members rotate keys simultaneously in two rounds (the MLS 'propose and commit' pattern) without the damage or cost of prior concurrent schemes (which either made later operations costlier or weakened PCS); low communication and PCS retained.
bitmessage_link: none direct

title: DeCAF: Decentralizable Continuous Group Key Agreement with Fast Healing
note: DeCAF: decentralisable concurrent CGKA with fast healing (users heal after at most log(t) requests, t being the number of corrupted users) and low communication cost, usable without a central server to order updates; improves on CoCoA's healing speed.
bitmessage_link: Decentralised group key agreement fits flooded or federated networks with no central sequencer.

title: On the Cost of Post-Compromise Security in Concurrent Continuous Group-Key Agreement
note: Examines the cost of post-compromise security in concurrent CGKA: sequential TreeKEM updates need all users to process previous updates; later TreeKEM versions allow concurrent updates at communication overhead linear in the number of concurrent updaters, and the paper gives bounds on what PCS costs under concurrency.
bitmessage_link: none direct

title: Continuous Group-Key Agreement: Concurrent Updates without Pruning
note: CGKA with concurrent updates but without pruning (not discarding concurrent updates); retains PCS with logarithmic cost.
bitmessage_link: none direct

title: Quarantined-TreeKEM: a Continuous Group Key Agreement for MLS, Secure in Presence of Inactive Users
note: Quarantined-TreeKEM: handles inactive users who would otherwise block PCS and FS in TreeKEM by putting them in quarantine; keeps the same security level for active members with limited extra cost.
bitmessage_link: Inactive members are common in asynchronous delivery; relevant to store-and-forward groups.

title: The Art of Bonsai: How Well-Shaped Trees Improve the Communication Cost of MLS
note: Improves MLS communication cost by choosing tree shapes: user add and tree expansion algorithms with better worst-case and average-case cost than the standard ones.
bitmessage_link: none direct

title: ETK: External-Operations TreeKEM and the Security of MLS in RFC 9420
note: Security proof for RFC 9420 TreeKEM including external operations (external commits and proposals) that earlier analyses of drafts omitted; ETK (External-Operations TreeKEM) models these and shows the final standard meets its goals, with some corrections.
bitmessage_link: none direct

title: Analyzing Group Chat Encryption in MLS, Session, Signal, and Matrix
note: Analyses the composition of symmetric encryption and signatures in the chat layers of MLS, Session, Signal and Matrix (symmetric signcryption formalism): practically exploitable replay and reordering attacks by a group insider in MLS and Session; a forgery attack by an outsider holding a user's signing key in Signal (previously found by Balbas et al.); Matrix is saved by ecosystem mitigations; gives security theorems for each construction up to those attacks and findings specific to Session.
bitmessage_link: Session is the Bitmessage-lineage messenger; the paper shows its group encryption has the same signature-binding weakness as peers.

title: Exploring How to Authenticate Application Messages in MLS: More Efficient, Post-Quantum, and Anonymous Blocklistable
note: Authentication of MLS application messages: replaces per-message EdDSA with more efficient, post-quantum and anonymously blocklistable alternatives; shows trade-offs between non-repudiation and deniability within groups.
bitmessage_link: Bitmessage signs every object; this line trades signatures against deniability and size.

title: Auditable Continuous Group Key Agreement
note: Auditable CGKA: lets a designated auditor recover past epoch keys and verify recovery remains possible, without a silent escrow; targets regulated sectors that otherwise log plaintext.
bitmessage_link: none direct

title: A Formal Analysis of Apple’s iMessage PQ3 Protocol
note: Formal verification (Tamarin) of Apple's iMessage PQ3: hybrid post-quantum initialisation then Signal-like ratchet with PQ rekeying; proves confidentiality, authentication, forward secrecy and post-compromise security (including post-quantum PCS) for the specified fine-grained compromise scenarios, and extracts the exact conditions and caveats (such as rekeying conditions) for PQ-PCS.
bitmessage_link: Gives a verified reference point for post-quantum session security in a production messenger.

title: Security analysis of the iMessage PQ3 protocol
note: Computational-model security analysis of PQ3: shows classical and post-quantum confidentiality with forward secrecy and post-compromise secrecy under reductions to underlying primitives; authentication remains classical.
bitmessage_link: none direct

title: CONIKS: Bringing Key Transparency to End Users
note: End-user key verification service: provider maintains a Merkle prefix tree of name-to-key bindings with signed tree roots chained in a hash chain; users self-monitor their own bindings in under 20 kB per day; detects equivocation without global third-party monitors; claims non-equivocation, privacy of names (VRF-based) and auditability.
bitmessage_link: Bitmessage's self-certifying addresses avoid a directory; CONIKS is the fix for directory-based messengers.

title: SEEMless: Secure End-to-End Encrypted Messaging with less trust
note: Auditable key directory supporting key changes (device loss) with privacy: append-only audit of a verifiable-random-function-hidden directory by untrusted auditors; claims soundness of lookups, history verification and no new info leak beyond lookups; more efficient audits than CONIKS-style designs.
bitmessage_link: none direct

title: Parakeet: Practical Key Transparency for End-to-End Encrypted Messaging
note: Practical key transparency for E2EE messaging (the design behind the WhatsApp Auditable Key Directory): scales to billions of users with a Merkle-tree directory, VRF-hidden usernames and efficient per-epoch auditing, with an out-of-band consistency protocol; reports performance for 'billions of users' and lower bandwidth than SEEMless.
bitmessage_link: none direct

title: Merkle^2: A Low-Latency Transparency Log System
note: Low-latency transparency log (Merkle^2) with auditing: cuts monitoring cost by two-layer Merkle trees so that updates take effect quickly (no hour-long wait); applies to key transparency for E2EE.
bitmessage_link: none direct

title: SoK: On the Security Goals of Key Transparency Systems
note: Surveys the key transparency literature and gives the first cryptographically sound formalisation of KT as an ideal functionality, identifying security goals (including previously unstated ones) and comparing designs (CONIKS, SEEMless, Parakeet, OPTIKS, Merkle^2).
bitmessage_link: none direct

title: Rotatable Zero Knowledge Sets: Post Compromise Secure Auditable Dictionaries with application to Key Transparency
note: Rotatable zero-knowledge sets: append-only ZK sets for privacy-preserving key transparency that can restore privacy after a server compromise (post-compromise security of the directory) while keeping auditability.
bitmessage_link: Post-compromise security for the key directory itself, the analogue of PCS for the session keys.

title: Signal and Ready to MINGLE: In-Band Gossip for Key Transparency Split-View Detection in E2EE Messengers
note: MINGLE: opportunistic in-band gossip of compact key-transparency commitments piggybacked on ordinary E2EE messages so that clients detect split-view equivocation without third-party auditors.
bitmessage_link: Uses message traffic itself as the gossip channel, much as a gossip or flooding overlay would.

title: Whom do you trust? PRISM: Lightweight Key Transparency for All
note: PRISM: lightweight key transparency with a zero-knowledge virtual machine 'rollup' on a third-party data availability layer so every user automatically checks the whole directory's integrity; claims large performance gains over custom ZK circuits.
bitmessage_link: Blockchain-style public append-only directory as the trust anchor, a direction relevant to chain-anchored messengers.

title: Consistency-or-Die: Consistency for Key Transparency
note: Consistency-or-Die: a consistency protocol protecting a key transparency log against split-view attacks without small committees of known auditors, out-of-band channels or blockchains, using a randomly selected, initially undisclosed committee of users (VRFs, key-evolving signatures) to endorse the log view; users know whether they are consistent and stop using the log if not.
bitmessage_link: Decentralised, user-run consistency checking instead of trusted auditors.

title: Weak Consistency mode in Key Transparency: OPTIKS
note: Adds an auditor-free mode to OPTIKS key transparency with slightly weaker security (weak consistency), formalised and proved.
bitmessage_link: none direct

title: Aegon: Self-Auditable Key Transparency
note: Aegon: key transparency whose server computation depends only on the updates in the current epoch (no per-epoch global invariance proofs), enabling short epochs and auditing by lightweight end users instead of global third-party auditors.
bitmessage_link: none direct

title: Forget-me-not Trees: Mass-scale Auditable Key Transparency from Hash Functions
note: Forget-me-not trees (Merkle trees plus Bloom filters): key transparency with audit proofs about 500x smaller (from 15-30 MB to 30-60 KB), relying only on hash functions.
bitmessage_link: none direct

title: OPTIKS: An Optimized Key Transparency System
note: OPTIKS: a full-featured key transparency system optimised for scalability (simpler and faster than prior designs, smaller storage overhead, crash-tolerant scalable server architecture) while keeping strong security and privacy notions; addresses real-world deployment issues.
bitmessage_link: none direct

title: ELEKTRA: Efficient Lightweight multi-dEvice Key TRAnsparency
note: Formalises the Multi-Device Verifiable Key Directory (MVKD) with completeness, extraction-based soundness and privacy, and gives ELEKTRA, combining the Keybase KT core with identity-key management across a user's devices so that devices can help monitor and prevent fake-key registration.
bitmessage_link: Multi-device key management for the directory, the device-level counterpart of Sesame's session management.

title: X-Wing: The Hybrid KEM You’ve Been Looking For
note: X-Wing hybrid KEM from X25519 and ML-KEM-768 with a SHA3-256 combiner; proves classical IND-CCA security under the strong DH assumption in the ROM and post-quantum IND-CCA security if ML-KEM-768 is IND-CCA and SHA3-256 is a PRF (standard model), so it is secure if either component is; efficiency gains rely on the specific component choices and do not generalise.
bitmessage_link: Practical hybrid KEM for replacing the classical ECDH step in static-key encryption.

title: KEM Combiners
note: Introduces KEM combiners: black-box constructions that take any set of ingredient KEMs and yield a KEM that is CCA-secure as long as at least one ingredient is, built from hash functions and key-derivation; the theoretical basis for hybrid classical/post-quantum KEMs in messaging.
bitmessage_link: Underpins mixing a post-quantum KEM with ECDH in a static key setup.

title: Hybrid Key Encapsulation Mechanisms and Authenticated Key Exchange
note: Models hybrid KEMs and hybrid authenticated key exchange with adversaries of varying quantum power over time (who may become quantum in the future or already are); gives generic combiner constructions and a hybrid AKE security definition including forward secrecy, the formal basis for PQ/T hybrid handshakes such as PQXDH and PQ3.
bitmessage_link: none direct

title: The Signal Private Group System and Anonymous Credentials Supporting Efficient Verifiable Encryption
note: Signal's private group system: group membership stored encrypted on the server, members authenticate with keyed-verification anonymous credentials (a new algebraic-MAC KVAC with group-element attributes, enabling efficient verifiable encryption) revealing only that they correspond to some encrypted entry; claims membership hidden from the service provider and outsiders while visible to members.
bitmessage_link: Hides group membership from the server, which Bitmessage achieves for chans by sharing one passphrase-derived key instead of any server-side membership list.

title: Hecate: Abuse Reporting in Secure Messengers with Sealed Sender
note: Hecate: asymmetric message franking compatible with sealed sender (sender-anonymous delivery): reporting of abusive messages to a moderator with accountability and deniability, plus forward and backward secrecy and combination with source tracing, in the plain model with fewer primitive calls than the CRYPTO 2019 construction.
bitmessage_link: Abuse handling compatible with sender anonymity, the same tension Bitmessage addresses with proof of work.

title: Formal Analysis of Session-Handling in Secure Messaging: Lifting Security from Sessions to Conversations
note: Formal analysis of the session-handling layer (Sesame) above the Double Ratchet: shows experimentally that PCS can be violated in Signal by a clone attacker even with the Double Ratchet because merging multiple ratchet chains into one conversation lets the attacker's session persist; designs a fix (and a Tamarin-verified model) restoring FS and PCS at the conversation level.
bitmessage_link: Conversation-level (not session-level) forward secrecy and PCS, the level that matters for a multi-device user of a store-and-forward system.

title: Secure Messaging with Strong Compromise Resilience, Temporal Privacy, and Immediate Decryption
note: First provably secure messaging protocol achieving at once strong resilience to fine-grained compromise, temporal privacy and immediate decryption with constant-size overhead, in the post-quantum setting; introduces a new offline-deniability definition that the protocol meets when combined with a post-quantum offline-deniable initial key exchange.
bitmessage_link: Temporal privacy (old messages stay private even if later keys leak) combined with immediate decryption is the design goal for out-of-order, store-and-forward delivery.

title: Universally Composable End-to-End Secure Messaging
note: UC model of Signal end-to-end secure messaging: an ideal functionality for messaging with a PKI and untrusted server against an adversary that controls the network and adaptively, momentarily compromises parties; captures Signal's forward secrecy and recovery of security and the exact conditions under which they break; decomposes Signal into PKI, continuous key exchange, epoch symmetric ratchets and AEAD functionalities that are realised and composed.
bitmessage_link: Composable definition of the properties a ratcheted channel gives, against which static-key designs can be compared.

title: Continuous Authentication in Secure Messaging
note: Authentication Steps extension for Signal-like protocols: continuous authentication during a session using users' long-term secrets (no out-of-band channel needed), guaranteeing authenticity while long-term secrets stay uncompromised, strengthening post-compromise security and allowing after-the-fact detection of long-term secret compromise; formal definition, general construction, proof and prototype.
bitmessage_link: Bitmessage addresses bind keys by hash but offer no ongoing authentication step; this adds authentication that heals.

title: Unique-Path Identity Based Encryption With Applications to Strongly Secure Messaging
note: Unique-Path IBE: a restricted hierarchical IBE sufficient for strongly secure messaging (strongly secure messaging protocols are equivalent to key-updatable KEMs, all prior constructions rely on adaptive unbounded-depth HIBE) with much better efficiency, enabling optimal-security messaging without the prohibitive HIBE cost.
bitmessage_link: none direct

title: How to Compare Bandwidth Constrained Two-Party Secure Messaging Protocols: A Quest for A More Efficient and Secure Post-Quantum Protocol
note: Proposes a pragmatic metric of how secure a messaging protocol is given a particular communication pattern, to compare bandwidth-constrained post-quantum protocols (PQ3, Triple Ratchet and new designs); shows there is no 'optimal' protocol since designs are incomparable under worst-case adversarial messaging behaviour with real bandwidth limits; develops a framework and a more efficient and secure PQ protocol.
bitmessage_link: Makes the bandwidth-versus-healing trade-off explicit, central for any flooded network.

title: Crypto Wars in Secure Messaging: Covert Channels in Signal Despite Leaked Keys
note: Anamorphic constructions embedding covert messages in the existing Signal Double Ratchet (in the DH keys of the asymmetric ratchet or in symmetric-ratchet authentication tags), letting users communicate covertly even against an adversary that can decrypt all Signal traffic (mandated access or leaked keys).
bitmessage_link: none direct

title: Verbeth: Secure Messaging with Metadata Minimization over Public Blockchain Logs
note: Private instant messaging that uses the public log layer of a blockchain as the transport while all cryptographic state stays in client apps; censorship resistant; first contact by long-term key encapsulation with trial decryption, or by a private signalling service on trusted hardware; for ongoing conversations, topic rotation driven by the off-chain session keys limits metadata leakage; studies economic and cryptographic limits of on-chain messaging.
bitmessage_link: A direct modern descendant of Bitmessage's flood-and-trial-decrypt design on a blockchain log, adding rotating topics and ratcheted session keys; the closest match to the Bitmessage problem in this slice.

title: Ilyazh-Web3E2E: A Post-Quantum Hybrid Protocol for Forward-Secure Decentralized Messaging
note: Proposes a post-quantum hybrid messaging protocol for Web3 identities: Double Ratchet extended with hybrid KEM (X25519 plus ML-KEM), hybrid authentication (Ed25519 plus ML-DSA) and re-encapsulation ratcheting; claims forward secrecy and post-compromise security; IND-CCA and AKE arguments are only sketched, with comparisons to PQXDH and PQ3 (single-author preprint without a full proof).
bitmessage_link: Decentralised-identity messaging with post-quantum hybrid ratcheting, a Bitmessage-like setting; security arguments are informal.

title: Symmetric Signcryption and E2EE Group Messaging in Keybase
note: Introduces symmetric signcryption (sender and recipient share a secret key) and proves that composing symmetric encryption and signatures achieves strong security against attackers learning and controlling many keys; models the core Keybase encrypted group messaging algorithm as symmetric signcryption and proves it secure under non-standard, brittle assumptions on the primitives; the model later used for MLS, Session, Signal and Matrix.
bitmessage_link: Chan-style shared-key groups with sender signatures are exactly this primitive (Bitmessage signs objects).

title: Device-Oriented Group Messaging: A Formal Cryptographic Analysis of Matrix’ Core
note: First formal description of Matrix's secure group messaging core in a new Device-Oriented Group Messaging model (users, devices and groups with shared state); proves Matrix meets confidentiality and authentication provided it adds authenticated group membership; shows Matrix's state-sharing (history sharing, account recovery) conflicts with forward secrecy and post-compromise security, raising questions about how those notions apply.
bitmessage_link: Matrix's room key sharing trades forward secrecy for history access, the same trade-off as long-lived chan keys.

title: Cryptographic Administration for Secure Group Messaging
note: Administrated CGKA (A-CGKA): extends continuous group key agreement so that only designated group admins can add or remove members and update keys, with a correctness notion and security definitions; gives cryptographic guarantees on group membership instead of leaving administration to the application layer, which loses confidentiality and consistency.
bitmessage_link: Chans in Bitmessage have no membership control; A-CGKA is the formal answer.

title: Membership Privacy for Asynchronous Group Messaging
note: Membership privacy for asynchronous group messaging: extends the ART protocol (Cohn-Gordon et al.) with key-private, robust public-key encryption to hide membership-related values from non-members, and uses properties of the group common key to avoid the per-member pairwise cost of Chase et al.'s Signal private groups, so the scheme scales better.
bitmessage_link: Hides group membership from outsiders (and the server) without pairwise fan-out, the property chans obtain from a shared secret.

title: The Key Lattice Framework for Concurrent Group Messaging
