note: Key lattice framework: a key-management layer for concurrent group messaging over secure pairwise channels, with simpler game-based definitions combining forward secrecy and post-compromise security into directional notions; handles concurrent updates natively.
bitmessage_link: Group key management over pairwise channels, matching deployments built from pairwise ratchets.

title: Formal Analysis of Multi-Device Group Messaging in WhatsApp
note: Formal description of WhatsApp's multi-device group messaging (from public documentation plus reverse engineering) in an extended Device-Oriented Group Messaging model with device revocation; states and proves the security guarantees it provides and discusses limitations of those guarantees.
bitmessage_link: Gives the precise formal guarantees of the largest group-messaging deployment, none of which exist for Bitmessage chans.

title: SoK: Multi-Device Secure Instant Messaging
note: Systematisation of multi-device secure instant messaging: patterns for data transfer between devices and device management (linking and unlinking devices to an account, initial setup), evaluated across messengers on security, usability and privacy goals; outlines research gaps.
bitmessage_link: Bitmessage has no device concept (keys are copied by hand), the gap this SoK catalogues.

title: Multi-Device for Signal
note: Multi-device extension of Signal with a formal security model: Sesame was not designed as a specific multi-device solution and has no security model; the paper defines multi-device secure instant messaging security and builds a protocol on the Double Ratchet that exploits the particular properties of the multi-device setting (all devices belong to one user) rather than a generic group key exchange.
bitmessage_link: Bitmessage identities are tied to one key set; multi-device needs this style of per-user device management.

title: Security under Message-Derived Keys: Signcryption in iMessage
note: Formalises Encryption under Message-Derived Keys (EMDK) and proves security of the EMDK scheme and the signcryption at the core of Apple's iMessage, with signcryption definitions extended for messaging issues; quantitative results and practical implications for iMessage (the pre-PQ3 protocol).
bitmessage_link: none direct

title: Privacy Failures in Encrypted Messaging Services:  Apple iMessage and Beyond
note: Shows an eavesdropper can learn user actions, message language and message length with over 96 percent accuracy from encrypted packet sizes in iMessage (and generic to other services), despite end-to-end and transport encryption.
bitmessage_link: Size side channel that padding or flooding of uniform-size objects (as in Bitmessage) avoids.

title: Impossibility Results for Post-Compromise Security in Real-World Communication Systems
note: Proves impossibility results for post-compromise security at the end-user level: although ratcheting protocols (iMessage, WhatsApp, Signal) have been proven to achieve PCS at the protocol level, communication systems with the usability features users need (such as multi-device, backups or restoring a state) cannot provide PCS against a compromise of such state; formalises conditions under which end users can obtain PCS.
bitmessage_link: Sets a ceiling on what PCS can mean in practice for users who copy keys between devices, as Bitmessage users must.

title: How fast do you heal? A taxonomy for post-compromise security in secure-channel establishment
note: Framework to quantify and compare post-compromise security through a taxonomy of adversaries: how many messages after compromise until the channel heals; models the healing speed of Signal, an identity-based messaging protocol (SAID) and even 5G handover compositions.
bitmessage_link: Provides the vocabulary to say that a static key never heals (infinite healing time).

title: How Secure is TextSecure?
note: First public security analysis of TextSecure (the Signal predecessor, protocol version 2): finds an unknown key-share attack on the key exchange and discusses other weaknesses of the then-new protocol including message authenticity, while rating the overall design strong; established the first targeted-analysis line of work on Signal.
bitmessage_link: Shows early analyses finding key-exchange flaws in a protocol far more scrutinised than Bitmessage's.

title: Post-quantum TLS without handshake signatures
note: KEMTLS: replaces handshake signatures with KEM-based authentication to cut post-quantum bandwidth (a size-optimised instantiation needs under half the bandwidth of post-quantum TLS 1.3) and server CPU (about 90 percent fewer cycles), with implicit authentication, weaker deniability-like properties and one extra round trip for explicit server authentication.
bitmessage_link: KEM-based authentication avoids per-message signatures, the direction suited to bandwidth-sensitive flooding networks.

title: Keeping Up with the KEMs: Stronger Security Notions for KEMs and Automated Analysis of KEM-based protocols
note: Stronger security notions for KEMs (binding of the shared secret to ciphertext and public key; the KEM binding property needed by PQXDH and similar protocols) and a symbolic analysis method (Tamarin) for protocols that use KEMs; shows relations between notions and applies them to protocols including Signal-style handshakes.
bitmessage_link: The KEM binding properties are what the PQXDH verification found missing; relevant to any post-quantum upgrade of static-key encryption.

title: CRYSTALS -- Kyber: a CCA-secure module-lattice-based KEM
note: CRYSTALS-Kyber: a CCA-secure module-lattice KEM (successor of NewHope) with key and ciphertext sizes about half those of NewHope; the scheme standardised (with changes) as ML-KEM in FIPS 203 and used in PQXDH, PQ3, SPQR and X-Wing.
bitmessage_link: Source of the ML-KEM sizes (about 1 kB) that dominate post-quantum overhead in flooded networks.

title: CRYSTALS -- Dilithium: Digital Signatures from Module Lattices
note: CRYSTALS-Dilithium: lattice signature scheme designed to be simple to implement securely against side-channel attacks with efficiency comparable to the best lattice signatures; became ML-DSA (FIPS 204), the leading post-quantum signature for messaging credentials.
bitmessage_link: Signature size is the obstacle for Bitmessage-style per-object signing in the post-quantum setting.

title: From Specs to Apps: Verifying and Monitoring Models of Signal and WhatsApp
note: Applies the SpecMon runtime monitor to WhatsApp Web and Signal Desktop to check whether observed executions conform to formal protocol models, bridging the gap between proven specifications and implementation behaviour.
bitmessage_link: none direct

title: Security Analysis of Signal's PQXDH Handshake
note: Game-based reductionist security analysis of Signal's PQXDH in a maximum-exposure model (fine-grained compromise of long-term, semi-static and ephemeral keys against classical and quantum adversaries), capturing the KEM component and the signing of public keys; establishes concrete security bounds for PQXDH.
bitmessage_link: none direct

title: A More Complete Analysis of the Signal Double Ratchet Algorithm
note: UC ideal functionality F_DR achieved by the Signal Double Ratchet that captures guarantees absent from the Cohn-Gordon et al. and Alwen-Coretti-Dodis analyses; constructs six modified DR variants that are insecure under F_DR yet secure under one or both earlier definitions, showing those definitions leave real gaps.
bitmessage_link: none direct

title: Better Security Proofs for X3DH and XHMQV
note: Tight security reductions for X3DH and its enhancement XHMQV under multi-user DH assumptions, so that concrete security with Curve25519 and XEdDSA approaches the intended 128-bit level instead of losing a factor in the number of sessions.
bitmessage_link: none direct
